title: The $18,000,000 Maple Syrup Heist
sources: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist' (2011-2012; about 2,700 tonnes stolen from the strategic reserve warehouse at Saint-Louis-de-Blandford, Quebec; valued at nearly $18 million; discovered in July 2012 when an inspector found a barrel that nearly fell over was light; other barrels held water; thieves siphoned syrup into their own barrels over about 10 months and refilled the empties with water; about 450 tonnes recovered; Richard Vallieres, the ringleader, sentenced to 7 years 10 months; four men convicted)

CBC News, '2 charged in $18M maple syrup heist' (18 Dec 2012) and 'Only in Canada? Seized maple syrup gets police protection' (4 Oct 2012) (barrels taken from the warehouse; 600+ barrels recovered in New Brunswick; investigation covered Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and the northern U.S.)

NPR, 'Thieves Hit Warehouse Holding $30 Million Of Canadian Maple Syrup' (31 Aug 2012) (the Federation of Quebec Maple Syrup Producers found the theft during a routine inventory check; the reserve exists to stabilise supply and price)

National Post, 'The great maple syrup heist: Trial opens...' (20 Oct 2016) (investigators: nearly 3,000 tonnes, valued at $18,721,000; RCMP, Canada Border Services Agency and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement assisted; more than 300 people interviewed, 40 search warrants)
A full barrel of maple syrup weighs about 270 kg (about 600 lb) (Canadian Encyclopedia, heist article)

lines.text: In 2012, someone stole eighteen million dollars of maple syrup.
lines.caps: In 2012, | someone stole | $18 million | of maple syrup

lines.text: And for almost a year, nobody noticed.
Quebec makes most of the world's maple syrup.
The federation keeps a strategic reserve:
a warehouse stacked with barrels,
in Saint-Louis-de-Blandford.
A full barrel weighs six hundred pounds.
The thieves never broke in.
They worked in the same industrial park.
Every night, they rolled a barrel out,
siphoned the syrup into their own barrels,
filled the empty one with water,
and rolled it back.
Ten months. Nobody checked.
Then July 2012: an inspector climbs the stack,
lines.caps: Then, | July 2012: | an inspector | climbs the stack,

lines.text: and one barrel almost falls over.
Too light. He opens it. It's water.
Police interview three hundred people,
and search forty locations.
They recover about four hundred fifty tonnes.
The rest was sold in Ontario and the U.S.
Four men went to prison.
The ringleader got nearly eight years.
And the reserve is still there.
The locks are better now.
Somewhere out there, someone is still eating the world's most expensive pancakes.
